comments.text:
One reason (IMO) that the US side of Lake Ontario hasn't been developed as much as the Canadian side is the prevailing wind.  Because of the generally eastward flow of air, the US side of Lake Ontario is regularly inundated with snow.  I mean, Toronto gets about 48-51 inches (120-130cm) of snow a year.  Rochester, which is about 100 miles southeast on the other side of the lake gets over 100 inches (~250cm) of snow a year, about twice as much.  Oswego, on the eastern edge as mentioned in the video, gets about 140 inches (~350cm) of snow a year.

Because of that, the cities in this region of NY clustered more around the Erie Canal - farther away from the lake vs the coast - and avoided more of the snow.  And the canal offered the cities on the US side more of an economic boon than Lake Ontario, because of the lack of a need to traverse Canadian waters.

Canada didn't decide that Lake Ontario 'was the best place to put its largest city'.  For 90% of post-contact history, until 1976, the largest city in Canada was Montreal, which was, for the most part, as far up the St. Lawrence as you can navigate prior to the construction of the Seaway.

1976 was also the year that Quebec elected its first separatist government.  Therein lies why Toronto overtook Montreal to become the largest city.

Canada isn't the only one to take 'advantage' of Lake Ontario.  Most of the shipping on the lakes is American.
